[[Bailie]] '''Hugh Blackburn''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|b|l|æ|k|b|ər|n}}) (2 July 1823 – 9 October 1909) was a Scottish mathematician. A lifelong friend of William Thomson (later [[Lord Kelvin]]) and the husband of illustrator [[Jemima Blackburn]], he was [[professor of mathematics at the University of Glasgow]] from 1849 to 1879. He succeeded Thomson's father [[James Thomson (mathematician)|James]] in the chair of mathematics.

==Life==
[[File:Hugh Blackburn2.jpg|thumb|An 1877 caricature of Hugh Blackburn|alt=An 1877 caricature of Hugh Blackburn|left|218x218px]]
Blackburn was born on 2 July 1823 in Craigflower, [[Torryburn]], [[Fife]]. He was brought up at [[Killearn House]], Stirlingshire, the seventh of eight children of wealthy Glasgow merchant John Blackburn and his wife Rebecca Leslie Gillies, the daughter of a [[Church of Scotland]] minister and a relative of [[Colin Maclaurin]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Blackburn.html|title=Hugh Blackburn|publisher=School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of St Andrews|accessdate=16 September 2010}}</ref> His elder brother was Judge [[Colin Blackburn, Baron Blackburn]]. His father became wealthy off sugar and slavery in Jamaica, becoming a merchant on his return to Glasgow. In the 1830s, when the British government emancipated the slaves, John received compensation for the ownership of over 550 slaves.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/lbs/person/view/20601|title = Summary of Individual &#124; Legacies of British Slavery}}</ref>

Blackburn was educated at the [[Edinburgh Academy]] and [[Eton College|Eton]] before entering [[Trinity College, Cambridge]] in 1840.<ref name=Venn>{{acad|id= BLKN840H|name=Blackburn, Hugh}}</ref> There he met Thomson, who entered in the same year; he was also a member of the [[Cambridge Apostles]]. During this time he invented the [[Blackburn pendulum]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.universitystory.gla.ac.uk/biography/?id=WH2092&type=P|title=Biography of Hugh Blackburn|publisher=University of Glasgow|accessdate=15 September 2010|archive-date=10 March 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120310143758/http://www.universitystory.gla.ac.uk/biography/?id=WH2092&type=P|url-status=dead}}</ref> In the [[Mathematical Tripos]] examinations of 1845 he graduated fifth [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|wrangler]], while Thomson graduated second wrangler.

He entered the [[Inner Temple]] in 1847 but was never called to the bar; his name was withdrawn in 1849, the year in which he became a professor of mathematics at the University of Glasgow.<ref name=Venn/> He married [[Jemima Blackburn|Jemima Wedderburn]] (cousin of [[James Clerk Maxwell]]), the daughter of [[James Wedderburn (judge)|James Wedderburn]], [[Solicitor General for Scotland]].<ref name="Venn" /> He died on 9 October 1909 at his estate in [[Roshven]], [[Inverness-shire]].[[File:Newton-5-3.jpg|alt=Title page in a 1871 copy of "Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica" by Isaac Newton, with dedication to Blackburn and William Thomson|thumb|242x242px|Title page in an 1871 copy of ''[[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica|Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica]]'' by [[Isaac Newton]], with a dedication to Blackburn and [[William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin|William Thomson]]]]

==Works==
*''A treatise on trigonometry'', London, 1855. Part of the ''[[Encyclopedia Metropolitana]]''.
*''A short sketch of the constitutional history of the University of Glasgow and of Glasgow College in that University: with remarks on the Universities (Scotland) Bill'', 1858
*(ed. with [[Lord Kelvin|William Thomson]] ) ''Sir [[Isaac Newton]]'s [[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica|Principia]]'', 1871
*''Elements of plane trigonometry for the use of the junior class of mathematics in the University of Glasgow'', 1871
